**Spirit and Opportunity — a 20 cm baseline, and a plain that gave stereo nothing to match (2004–2006)**

NASA's twin Mars Exploration Rovers carried a mast-mounted navigation stereo pair with a 20 cm baseline and a 45-degree field of view, and their onboard Visual Odometry compared 256 x 256 stereo pairs taken at successive stops, tracking autonomously selected terrain features to correct a pose estimate that wheel encoders and the IMU could not be trusted to supply. JPL's published results are unusually frank about both halves of the bargain. The system detected slip ratios as high as 125%, measured changes as small as 2 mm, and held up on slopes tilted as much as 31 degrees.

The baseline is the whole argument. With Z = fb/d, depth uncertainty grows as Z²/(fb), so 20 cm of separation buys usable geometry inside the rover's own working volume and very little past it. That is the right trade for a vehicle localising against terrain a few metres ahead: the near field is where a short baseline is strongest and where the occluded band visible to only one camera is narrowest. A longer bar would have bought range the rover had no use for and paid for it in occlusion and mounting stiffness.

The failure mode was texture, not geometry. Opportunity worked Meridiani Planum, and JPL reported that the flat, featureless landscape made machine stereo correlation between the left and right eyes difficult. Across two years, Visual Odometry converged on 97% of attempts on Spirit and 95% on Opportunity; on sol 235 one of the few outright failures was attributed to a lack of useful visual features. This is the quiet kind of failure — a bland cost curve does not report an error, it returns a minimum, and a sub-pixel parabola fitted to a nearly flat curve returns a confident number about nothing. In April 2005 Opportunity dug itself into a ripple later named Purgatory Dune, with wheel odometry reporting progress that was not happening; the rover was not driven clear until early June.

The fix cost time. Each Visual Odometry step took close to three minutes on the 20 MHz RAD6000, so it was commanded selectively — short drives, typically under 15 m, on slopes over roughly 10 degrees, when a wheel was being dragged, or through sand. Trustworthy localisation was bought with metres per sol.

When you specify a stereo rig you are fixing your working volume and your failure mode in the same decision. Before you tune SGM penalties, ask what your scene's texture actually looks like at the ranges that matter, instrument the cost curve rather than only the disparity, keep the left-right check as a gate rather than a diagnostic, and decide up front what the system does when disparity is unavailable — which is survivable — instead of quietly wrong, which is not.

**Notre-Dame de Paris — a billion points that recorded the building's errors rather than its drawings (2010–2019)**

In 2010 the art historian Andrew Tallon and Columbia's Paul Blaer spent five days inside Notre-Dame with a Leica ScanStation C10 on a tripod, repositioning it around 50 times to reach every accessible corner. National Geographic reported the result as more than a billion points collected from over 50 locations in and around the cathedral, accurate to within five millimetres.

The hard part of a campaign like this is not acquisition, it is registration. Each station produces a cloud in its own frame; every one has to be brought into a single datum, which is why markers were placed through the space before scanning. Target-based alignment sets the datum, and any residual then propagates along the chain of stations. A bad registration does not raise an error — it appears as a doubled surface, a wall that measures two centimetres thicker than it is. ICP will refine an alignment that is already close; it cannot rescue one that has drifted, and on repetitive Gothic geometry a point-to-point objective will happily settle into a locally consistent, globally wrong minimum.

What the cloud bought was measured reality instead of idealised drawing. Tallon's scans showed the Gallery of Kings on the west front standing almost a foot — about 0.3 m — out of plumb, and interior columns that do not line up because medieval builders worked around what was already standing. No elevation drawing contains that. It is only visible because the instrument records where the stone is, not where it was meant to be.

The cost is what a cloud is not. It is a set of samples of line-of-sight surfaces from 50 viewpoints: roof voids, vault extrados and anything occluded are absent, and absence looks identical to empty space. Normals must be estimated by local PCA over a neighbourhood you choose, then oriented against the sensor position, and that neighbourhood radius is a direct trade between smoothing noise and blunting the arrises that make the geometry legible. Voxel downsampling to a size any downstream tool can handle discards the sub-centimetre detail that justified the survey. After the 2019 fire the data became a reference for restoration, but it documents a prior state — the burnt structure had moved.

When you plan a scan campaign, your registration error budget is fixed by station placement and target layout before a single ICP iteration runs. Decide your voxel size, your normal-estimation neighbourhood and your outlier criterion against the smallest feature you are contracted to represent, and record which surfaces were never observed, because a downstream model will otherwise treat the gaps as fact.

**The Great Buddha of Bamiyan — four tourist snapshots against three survey plates from 1970 (2001–2004)**

The Taliban destroyed the two standing Buddhas of the Bamiyan valley in March 2001; the larger was 53 m high. Starting that July, the Institute of Geodesy and Photogrammetry at ETH Zurich — Armin Grün, Fabio Remondino and Li Zhang — attempted to reconstruct the Great Buddha from whatever imagery survived, running several data sets in parallel. Of 15 images found on the internet, four were selected for processing: two taken in front of the statue, one from the left and one from the right. Separately they had metric photographs taken in 1970.

The internet set is the pure incremental SfM problem with every convenience removed. Intrinsics unknown, poses unknown, scale unknown, and only four views with wide, uncontrolled angular separation between them — which is exactly the regime where self-calibration is weakest, because focal length and depth trade against each other and a bundle adjustment can absorb an error in one as a plausible value of the other. The team reported that internet images lack the photogrammetric information automated methods depend on, and that variations in illumination and in acquisition time left the resulting point cloud incomplete, with gaps where dense matching could find no consistent appearance across views. A reconstruction of this kind converges; it is self-consistent; it is not metric.

The 1970 metric photographs were a different instrument entirely. Three calibrated plates, geometry known rather than inferred, produced a reconstruction with an accuracy of 1–2 cm in relative position and an object resolution of about 5 cm. Even then the automation was not sufficient: manual image measurement had to be applied because the automatic procedures could not extract all the fine detail. From that cloud, ETH milled a 1:200 physical statue about 25 cm high on a Starrag NF100.

The honest conclusion in the work is the part worth carrying: the results derived from internet and tourist imagery were held to serve scientific purposes, not to stand as the metric record. Crowd-sourced photographs buy coverage of objects that no longer exist, and the price is calibration, scale and completeness. Three calibrated plates beat fifteen uncontrolled ones, and beat them by an order of magnitude.

When you point an incremental pipeline at an unordered collection, decide first which artefact you owe: something plausible, or something measurable. Check the initialisation pair for genuine parallax, watch whether the reconstruction drifts as images register, and establish before you start where scale and control will come from — because if the answer is nowhere, no amount of bundle adjustment will supply it.

**Cruise — the object was tracked correctly, then placed on the wrong side of the car (2023–2024)**

On the evening of 2 October 2023 in San Francisco, a human-driven Nissan struck a pedestrian crossing against a red light and threw her into the path of a Cruise robotaxi travelling in the adjacent lane. The perception stack was not blind. The independent review commissioned from Quinn Emanuel, with engineering analysis by Exponent, records that before the first impact the AV accurately detected, classified and tracked both the pedestrian and the human-driven vehicle. It braked hard; the analysis puts the AV at 18.6 mph at impact, down from 19.1 mph at detection.

The damage came from what happened to the position estimate at the instant of contact. The Exponent analysis states that the collision detection system incorrectly identified the pedestrian as being located on the side of the AV at the time of impact instead of in front of it. That single geometric error selected the wrong post-collision behaviour: classified as a side impact, the event routed to a minimal-risk-condition pullover rather than a stop in lane. The vehicle then moved off with the woman beneath it, travelling approximately 20 feet at up to 7.7 mph. It was configured to pull over as far as 100 feet, and stopped early only because a wheel speed sensor failed when the wheel turned on her leg.

Two failure layers stack here, and they are different problems. The first is a detection whose class was right and whose pose was wrong — the kind of error a mean-AP figure at a fixed 3D IoU threshold barely registers, because a box displaced from front to side still overlaps something and the aggregate metric averages it away. The second is coverage: once a person is under the vehicle she is not a hard case for the classifier, she is outside the sensor geometry altogether, in the region every perception stack implicitly assumes is empty.

California's DMV suspended the deployment permits, and Cruise later agreed to a $500,000 penalty over a false report about the incident to federal regulators. The published post-mortems put more weight on the response than on the perception error: a localisation error of roughly a vehicle width became a company-ending event through the behaviour it triggered.

The question this lesson prepares you to ask is not what your detector's AP is. It is which downstream behaviours read box centre and heading as a control input, and what each of them does when that box is off by a metre or flipped by ninety degrees. Trace those paths deliberately, treat heading ambiguity and coordinate-frame handoffs as safety-relevant rather than cosmetic, and define explicitly what happens when an object leaves the sensors' field of view rather than the scene.

**3D Gaussian Splatting — real-time radiance fields bought by throwing the network away (2023)**

At SIGGRAPH 2023, Bernhard Kerbl, Georgios Kopanas, Thomas Leimkühler and George Drettakis published "3D Gaussian Splatting for Real-Time Radiance Field Rendering" in ACM Transactions on Graphics. The abstract makes an unusually testable claim for this corner of the field: high-quality real-time novel-view synthesis at 30 fps or better, at 1080p, for unbounded and complete scenes — a combination the authors state no method had then achieved.

The alpha-compositing formula is retained; what is discarded is the queried MLP. Instead of marching a ray and evaluating a network at every sample, the scene is represented by explicit anisotropic 3D Gaussians, initialised from the sparse points that SfM camera calibration already produced, with interleaved optimisation and density control over their positions, covariances and opacities. A visibility-aware tile rasteriser then splats them. The consequence follows directly from the volume-rendering derivation: no compute is spent in empty space because there is nothing there to evaluate, and both training and rendering accelerate together rather than trading against each other.

The price is stated in the paper's own limitations. Memory consumption is significantly higher than NeRF-based solutions, and peak GPU memory during optimisation of large scenes can exceed 20 GB. Quality is not uniform: regions the cameras observed poorly produce elongated or splotchy Gaussians, and popping artefacts appear when optimisation creates large Gaussians in view-dependent regions — the authors attribute this partly to trivial rejection of Gaussians through a guard band in the rasteriser. Reported comparisons on Mip-NeRF360 place the 30k-iteration configuration in the region of half an hour of training, against Instant-NGP's roughly five to seven minutes.

Be careful about what was demonstrated. This is a rendering result, not a geometry result: nothing here extracts a surface, poses still come from an SfM pipeline that can fail on exactly the scenes you care about, and the representation remains per-scene. A large follow-on literature on compressing trained scenes is itself evidence that the raw form is not deployable as published.

The decision this lesson prepares you for is not "NeRF or Gaussians". It is what you are willing to store and what you need to be able to edit. Explicit primitives give you real-time rendering and a scene you can cull, move and prune; an implicit field gives you compactness and continuity where you have few observations. Benchmark at your own capture density and output resolution rather than on published scenes, because both methods degrade in the sparse-view regime and neither degrades gracefully.
